title: More Chicago Sky drama as Skylar Diggins airs frustration over her role
content:
The Chicago Sky can’t escape the drama.

General manager Jeff Pagliocca traded away former franchise cornerstone Angel Reese a month before the season started in an effort to move forward into a new era, but the instability remains. Leading up to Chicago’s game Tuesday against the Phoenix Mercury, veteran guard Skylar Diggins was informed she would be removed from the starting lineup. She responded by posting on her Instagram story Monday morning, “Now I’m coming off the bench?????? Cool”

Diggins told reporters Monday, according to the Chicago Sun-Times: “I’ve been putting my body on the line. I’m here for this team. I’ve done everything that’s been asked of me. I’ve been great professionally. That’s the decision that’s made, and I’ve got to live with that.”

Coach Tyler Marsh confirmed his decision to move Diggins to the bench but declined further comment, saying he wants to keep his conversations with players private.

Diggins, a 12-year WNBA veteran, is in her first season with the Sky. She has started all 19 games for Chicago and hasn’t come off the bench for any team since her fourth professional season with the Dallas Wings in 2016.

But her Chicago tenure has been bumpy. After a 3-1 start, the Sky have gone 3-13. Diggins’ assist percentage is on track with her All-Star campaigns, but her defense has regressed and her true shooting percentage (.515) is its lowest since 2016, despite shooting 38.2 percent on 3-pointers.

Diggins’ move to the second unit shouldn’t come as much of a surprise. Chicago already had veteran guard Courtney Vandersloot, who was a key piece of the franchise’s lone title in 2021, under contract when Diggins signed. Although Vandersloot was rehabbing a torn ACL suffered in June 2025 at the start of the season, the expectation was that the Sky icon would eventually return to the starting lineup. She has been back for three games, averaging 8.7 points and six assists in 16 minutes off the bench.

Vandersloot said before the season that she expected she and Diggins would be able to share the floor. Although both players are point guards, they have complementary skill sets with Vandersloot functioning more as a pure passer and Diggins adding some rim pressure to her playmaking.

However, as Diggins’ paint game has suffered in 2026 and rookie guard Sydney Taylor has emerged as a perimeter threat — she is averaging 16.4 points on 47 percent shooting when she starts — Diggins’ fit in the starting lineup has become less ideal.

Diggins expressed concern with the direction of the team long before her benching. After an 85-68 loss to Toronto on June 7, she responded to questions about the team’s offensive struggles by saying: “That’s a Tyler question. Ask Tyler.” She also called out the team’s need to shed its “loser mentality.”

Now, Chicago has a disgruntled veteran guard who still has $940,000 guaranteed on her contract for next season. The Sky could explore trade offers for Diggins, but they are on a win-now timeline.

A seven-time All-Star, Diggins has experienced friction at previous WNBA stops. She and Diana Taurasi had to be separated during an altercation on the bench when the two were teammates with the Phoenix Mercury in 2022; Diggins missed the last four games of the regular season and the postseason and had her contract temporarily suspended. She sat out the entire 2023 season on maternity leave and left the Mercury afterward for Seattle.

Diggins cited then-Storm star Jewell Loyd’s presence in Seattle as one of the reasons she wanted to join the Storm in 2024. The two Notre Dame guards were set to form a dynamic backcourt in Seattle to revitalize the franchise after a season out of the playoffs; instead, within a year, Loyd requested a trade.

Chicago also has experience dealing with players who publicly air their frustrations with the franchise.

Last season, Reese was benched for the first half of a game for “comments detrimental to the team” after she told the Chicago Tribune she wanted the Sky to obtain better talent in the offseason. The Sky held her out of the final three games with a back injury, and she was traded to the Atlanta Dream in April for future draft picks.

Now the Sky are dealing with another sticky situation.

This is a situation of Chicago’s own making, after it chose to roster three veteran point guards with strong personalities. In only his second year as a head coach, Marsh is again helming a combustible team that requires him to manage a lot more than just basketball.
